result.summary: Pausanias finishes his account of the Arcadians' history, from Troy to the Achæan League. He then begins describing the routes from Argolis into Arcadia and the sights along them near Mantinea.

scenes.title: Arcadian history in outline
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the wars the Arcadians fought in and their shifting loyalties to Lacedæmonians, Thebans and Macedonians.

scenes.title: Ladder pass and Meliastæ
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the passes into Arcadia, then the road from Melangea to the well of the Meliastæ with its sanctuaries of Dionysus and Aphrodite Melænis.

scenes.title: Artemisium and the Inachus
scenes.summary: The narrower pass over Artemisium holds the sources of the Inachus, which marks the Argive-Mantinean border.

alias_notes.explanation: Means Black; Pausanias explains it as love being pursued at night.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias' memorable explanation of Aphrodite's title 'Black'.

analysis.text: The summary shows Arcadia as a small inland people repeatedly caught between Sparta, Thebes, Macedon and the Achæan League.
Pausanias moves from history to travel guide, tying places to cult and local explanation.

language_notes.text: Ilium is Troy; the war against it is the Trojan War. The Medes here are the Persians, defeated at Platæa in 479 BC.
Chæronea (338 BC) was where Philip of Macedon defeated the Greek allies; the Thessalian action against Antipater is the Lamian War (323–322 BC).
The Galati are the Gauls, who invaded Greece in 279 BC and were resisted at Thermopylæ.
The Achæan League was a federation of Peloponnesian cities, powerful in the third and second centuries BC.
A stade was a Greek measure of length, about 180–200 metres, so seven stades is under a mile and a half.
Orgies here means secret religious rites, not the modern sense; Dionysus was honoured with such ritual.

context_notes.text: Thebes crushed Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC, and the Arcadians then turned to Theban leadership, founding Megalopolis as a check on Sparta.
Æschylus, the Athenian tragedian, uses the Inachus, Argos' river, as a poetic name for the Argive land and its people.

literary_notes.text: The contrast of compulsion and choice portrays the Arcadians as reluctant allies of Sparta, setting up their later change of side.
Pausanias explains a cult title by rational conjecture, treating the goddess's epithet Black as arising from human habit rather than myth.
